## Definition

The **median** is the middle value in an ordered dataset. Half the values fall below the median and half fall above. It represents the 50th percentile.

## Calculation

For odd number of values:

1. Order values from lowest to highest
2. Median = the middle value

For even number of values:

1. Order values from lowest to highest
2. Median = average of the two middle values

## Formula

$$Median = X_{\frac{n+1}{2}}$$ (for odd n)

$$Median = \frac{X_{\frac{n}{2}} + X_{\frac{n}{2}+1}}{2}$$ (for even n)

## Properties

| Property | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| Robust | Resistant to outliers |
| Positional | Based on rank, not values |
| Ordinal or above | Works with ranked data |
| Distribution-free | No assumptions about shape |

## When to Use the Median

The median is most appropriate when:

- Data are skewed
- Outliers are present
- Ordinal scale measurement
- Reporting "typical" values

## Example

Dataset: 2, 5, 7, 8, 12, 15, 150

- Mean = 28.4 (pulled up by outlier 150)
- Median = 8 (not affected by outlier)

The median better represents the typical value.

## R Code Example

```r
# Calculate median
median(scores)

# Median with missing values
median(scores, na.rm = TRUE)

# Compare mean and median to detect skew
mean(scores) > median(scores)  # TRUE suggests positive skew
```

## Visual Comparison with Mean

```
         Positively Skewed Distribution
         (e.g., reaction times, income)
              ▲
             ╱╲
            ╱  ╲
           ╱    ╲
          ╱      ╲────
         ╱            ─────
──────────────────────────────►
           │     │
         Median Mean

         Median < Mean = Positive skew
         Median > Mean = Negative skew
         Median ≈ Mean = Symmetric
```

## DataLab Connection

Reaction time data from the **Reflex Test** and **Time Warp** stations typically show positive skew. Report the median for a more accurate representation of "typical" performance.
